Recursion bottoms out at arrays of size 1
Merge the two sorted halves: repeatedly pick the smaller of the two front elements
After all levels complete, the full array is sorted

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Python's sorted() and list.sort() are based on Timsort, which builds on Merge Sort
Java's Arrays.sort(Object[]) uses Timsort (a Merge Sort variant)
External sorting — merging sorted file chunks when data is larger than memory
Linked list sorting — Merge Sort works with O(1) extra memory on linked lists
Git's 3-way merge is conceptually similar to the merge step in Merge Sort

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Quick Sort — faster on average and in-place, but worst case O(n²). Merge Sort always O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra memory
Heap Sort — also O(n log n) guaranteed and in-place, but poor cache locality can make it slower than Merge Sort in practice
Timsort — a hybrid of Merge Sort + Insertion Sort. Exploits pre-sorted runs in real-world data for exceptional performance

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Merge Sort is always O(n log n) regardless of input data
The split depth is log₂(n), and n elements are merged at each depth
Unlike Quick Sort, it requires O(n) extra memory
Being a stable sort means equal values keep their original order

items.q: How does it differ from Quick Sort?
items.a: Merge Sort is always O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra memory. Quick Sort averages O(n log n) with worst case O(n²) but sorts in-place with O(1) extra memory.

items.q: Why does stable sorting matter?
items.a: When sorting a database by name then by age, a stable sort preserves the name order for equal ages. Python's sorted() and Java's Arrays.sort(Objects) are merge sort-based.

items.q: When should I use Merge Sort?
items.a: When you need stable sorting, guaranteed worst-case performance, or sorting linked lists (where it uses O(1) extra memory).

quadTreeVisualizer.title: Quad Tree Visualizer
quadTreeVisualizer.description: Watch how 2D space is recursively divided into quadrants for efficient point management and range search

stepsGuide.description: Observe how points are inserted and space is subdivided.

whatIs.title: What is a Quad Tree?
whatIs.description: A Quad Tree is a spatial data structure that recursively divides 2D space into four quadrants to efficiently store and search point data. It is widely used in game collision detection, map systems, image compression, and more.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Click the canvas to add points manually, or use Random/Clustered buttons
Adjust node capacity (default 4) to change subdivision frequency
In Build mode, watch points being inserted and space being divided
In Search mode, observe how only points within the green area are found efficiently
Skipped nodes (red dashed) are areas that don't need to be checked

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Create a root node defining the entire 2D boundary
When a point is added, insert it into the appropriate quadrant
When a node exceeds its capacity, split into four children (NW, NE, SW, SE)
Dense areas are subdivided deeper; empty areas are never split
Range search: recursively visit only quadrants that overlap the query region

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Game collision detection — partition space so only nearby objects are tested against each other
Map services (Google Maps) — spatial indexing of points of interest (POIs)
Image compression — represent uniform-color regions as single nodes
N-body simulations — Barnes-Hut algorithm approximates distant bodies as one
GIS (Geographic Information Systems) — spatial data indexing

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: KD-Tree — alternates splitting axis each level; better for nearest-neighbor search but harder to update dynamically
R-Tree — groups rectangular regions hierarchically; the standard spatial index in databases (PostGIS)
Octree — Quad Tree extended to 3D; used for spatial partitioning in 3D games and simulations
Uniform Grid — divides space equally; simpler to implement but inefficient when data density varies greatly

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Set capacity to 1 to see subdivisions happen at every point insertion
With clustered patterns, notice how only certain areas are deeply subdivided
More skipped nodes in range search means more efficient searching
Quad trees work best when points are evenly distributed

items.q: Where are Quad Trees used?
items.a: Game collision detection (only compare nearby objects), map/GIS systems (regional search), image compression, and particle simulations.

items.q: What's a good node capacity?
items.a: Usually 4-16 is appropriate. Too small makes the tree deep, too large reduces search efficiency.

items.q: What's the time complexity?
items.a: Balanced case: insert/search O(log n), worst case (all points in one spot) O(n). Range search averages O(√n + k), much faster than O(n) brute force.

minimaxVisualizer.title: Minimax Game AI Visualizer
minimaxVisualizer.description: Learn Minimax algorithm and alpha-beta pruning through tic-tac-toe game trees

stats.nodeLimitHit: Node limit (3,000) reached — tree was truncated. Place more pieces on the board to see the full tree.
stats.tooManyEmpty: Too many empty cells — the tree will be very large. Place 3-4+ pieces before running for a cleaner visualization.

explain.idleDesc: Place pieces on the board and press ▶ to start
explain.expandDesc: Checking what happens if {player} plays cell {move} (depth {depth})
explain.winXDesc: Score +{score} — faster wins get higher scores
explain.winODesc: Score {score} — faster wins get lower scores
explain.backpropMaxDesc: Picks the highest score {score} among children
explain.backpropMinDesc: Picks the lowest score {score} among children
explain.pruneDesc: α({alpha}) ≥ β({beta}) → no need to search further

stepsGuide.description: Observe how the game tree is explored and scores propagate upward.

whatIs.title: What is the Minimax Algorithm?
whatIs.description: Minimax finds the optimal strategy in two-player zero-sum games. One player (MAX) tries to maximize the score while the opponent (MIN) tries to minimize it. Adding alpha-beta pruning cuts branches that can't affect the result, greatly speeding up the search.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Click the board to place X and O alternately (set up initial position)
Or use preset buttons for empty/mid-game/near-end states
Toggle alpha-beta pruning on/off to compare the difference
Press play to watch the game tree being built step by step
Orange nodes are MAX (maximizing), blue nodes are MIN (minimizing)

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Game states are represented as a tree: each node is a board position, each edge is a possible move
The maximizing player (MAX) picks the move with the highest score; the minimizing player (MIN) picks the lowest
Leaf nodes (game-over states) are evaluated and assigned a win/loss/draw score
Scores propagate back up: MAX nodes take the maximum child score, MIN nodes take the minimum
Alpha-beta pruning: if α (best MAX can guarantee) ≥ β (best MIN can guarantee), skip remaining children

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Chess/Go AI — foundation of Deep Blue (IBM) and AlphaGo; in practice combined with MCTS
Board game apps (Othello, Checkers, Connect4) for AI opponents
Card game AI (Poker, Hearts) — adapted variants handle imperfect information
Game theory in economics — modeling strategic decision-making in zero-sum scenarios
Automated negotiation systems — determining optimal offer/acceptance strategies

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: MCTS (Monte Carlo Tree Search) — uses random simulations to statistically evaluate promising moves; used by AlphaGo; better suited for large games like Go
Negamax — a simplified Minimax variant that eliminates the MAX/MIN distinction by negating scores at each level; cleaner to implement
Expectiminimax — extends Minimax to games with chance elements (dice, cards) by adding probability nodes

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Compare node counts with alpha-beta ON vs OFF on an empty board
Near-end positions have smaller trees, making it easier to follow the process
Pruned nodes (gray) are skipped because they can't change the result
MAX nodes choose the highest child score, MIN nodes choose the lowest

items.q: What games use Minimax?
items.a: All two-player perfect-information zero-sum games: chess, Go, Gomoku, checkers, etc. The Gomoku, Othello, and Connect4 AIs on this site are also Minimax-based.

items.q: Does alpha-beta pruning change the result?
items.a: No. Pruning only speeds up the search — the final result (optimal move) is identical. It simply skips unnecessary branches.

items.q: What's the optimal strategy in Tic-Tac-Toe?
items.a: If both players play optimally, it's always a draw. Minimax proves this — the root score becomes 0 (draw).

quickSortVisualizer.title: Quick Sort Visualizer
quickSortVisualizer.description: Watch the pivot-based partitioning and recursive sorting process

stepsGuide.description: Observe the pivot selection and partitioning process step by step.

whatIs.title: What is Quick Sort?
whatIs.description: Quick Sort is a high-performance sorting algorithm that uses the divide-and-conquer strategy. It selects a pivot element, partitions the array into elements smaller and larger than the pivot, then recursively sorts each partition. It has an average time complexity of O(n log n).

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Adjust the array size with the slider (5-50)
Generate different inputs with Random, Nearly Sorted, or Reversed buttons
The purple bar is the current pivot
The light purple background shows the current partition range
Green bars are elements in their final confirmed position

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Select a pivot — typically the last element, a random element, or the median of three
Partition: move elements smaller than the pivot to the left, larger to the right
Place the pivot in its correct final position
Recursively apply the same process to the left and right sub-arrays
Terminate when a sub-array has 1 or fewer elements

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Foundation of C's qsort() and Java's Arrays.sort() for primitive types
Default choice for sorting large datasets — average O(n log n) with excellent cache performance
Used in database engine sort operations
The canonical divide-and-conquer example taught in algorithms courses
Parallel Quick Sort — the left and right partitions can be sorted independently in parallel

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Merge Sort vs Quick Sort — Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) but requires O(n) extra memory. Quick Sort is in-place but has worst case O(n²)
Heap Sort — also O(n log n) guaranteed and in-place, but poor cache locality makes it slower than Quick Sort in practice
Introsort — a hybrid of Quick Sort + Heap Sort. Switches to Heap Sort when recursion depth exceeds a threshold to guarantee O(n log n) worst case. Used by C++ std::sort

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Once a pivot is placed, its position is final (it never moves again)
Choosing the last element as pivot on a reversed array triggers worst case (O(n²))
Deeper recursion means smaller sub-arrays are being processed
Random arrays show near-average O(n log n) performance

items.q: Is Quick Sort a stable sort?
items.a: No. Both Lomuto and Hoare partition schemes don't preserve the relative order of equal elements. Use Merge Sort if stability is needed.

items.q: What's the time complexity?
items.a: Average O(n log n), worst case O(n²) (sorted array + end pivot). Random or median-of-three pivot selection avoids worst case.

items.q: How does it compare to Bubble Sort?
items.a: Quick Sort is much faster on average (O(n log n) vs O(n²)). It's one of the most widely used sorting algorithms in practice.

bubbleSortVisualizer.title: Bubble Sort Visualizer
bubbleSortVisualizer.description: Watch adjacent elements being compared and swapped through bar chart animation

stepsGuide.description: Observe which elements are compared and swapped at each step.

whatIs.title: What is Bubble Sort?
whatIs.description: Bubble Sort is the most fundamental sorting algorithm that repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. The name comes from the way larger values 'bubble up' to the end of the array.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Adjust the array size with the slider (5-50)
Generate different inputs with Random, Nearly Sorted, or Reversed buttons
Press play to watch the sorting process step by step
Yellow means comparing, red means swapping, green means sorted
The Code tab highlights the current line being executed

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Compare adjacent elements from the start to the end of the array
If the left element is greater than the right, swap them
After one pass, the largest value has bubbled to the end
Repeat passes until no swaps occur
Time complexity: best O(n), average/worst O(n²)

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Simple sorting of small datasets (10 or fewer elements) that are nearly in order
Educational purposes — the classic first algorithm for teaching sorting concepts
Embedded systems with tight memory constraints (in-place, zero extra memory)
Maintaining sorted order in a real-time data stream with one pass after each new insertion

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Insertion Sort vs Bubble Sort — both O(n²), but Insertion Sort is 2–3× faster in practice (fewer comparisons). Prefer Insertion Sort for nearly-sorted data
Selection Sort — at most O(n) swaps, but comparisons are always O(n²). Bubble Sort can exit early with the early-termination optimization
Cocktail Shaker Sort — a bidirectional variant of Bubble Sort that alleviates the 'turtle problem' (small values near the end take many passes to reach the front)

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Notice how reversed arrays require maximum comparisons and swaps (O(n²))
Nearly sorted arrays finish quickly thanks to early termination optimization
Each pass moves the largest unsorted element to its correct position
If no swaps occur in a pass, the array is already sorted

items.q: Is Bubble Sort used in practice?
items.a: Rarely. Its O(n²) time complexity makes it inefficient for large datasets, but it's useful for learning algorithms and small datasets.

items.q: What's the time complexity?
items.a: Best case O(n) (already sorted), average and worst case O(n²). Space complexity is O(1) as it sorts in-place.

items.q: Is it a stable sort?
items.a: Yes, the relative order of equal elements is preserved. This is one of Bubble Sort's advantages.

aStarVisualizer.title: A* Pathfinding Visualizer
aStarVisualizer.description: Learn the A* (A-Star) shortest path algorithm through interactive visualization

stepsGuide.description: Observe how A* selects the node with the lowest cost.
stepsGuide.astarDescription: A* prioritizes nodes with the lowest f = g + h (actual cost + estimated cost).

whatIs.title: What is the A* Algorithm?
whatIs.description: A* (A-Star) is an algorithm that efficiently finds the shortest path in a graph. It extends Dijkstra's algorithm by adding a heuristic (estimated distance to goal) to guide the search direction. It is widely used in game AI, robot navigation, and GPS routing.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Click/drag on the grid to draw or erase walls
Set the start point (green) and goal point (red)
Choose a heuristic type (Manhattan/Euclidean/Chebyshev)
Enable diagonal movement for 8-directional search
Toggle cost display to see f/g/h values in each cell
Use A* vs BFS mode to compare efficiency

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Add the start node to the open list (priority queue) and compute f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the actual cost from start and h(n) is the heuristic estimate to goal.
Pop the node with the lowest f-value as the current node. If it's the goal, backtrack the path and exit.
Update g-values for neighboring nodes and update parent pointers when a better path is found.
Repeat until the open list is empty (no path exists) or the goal is reached.

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Real-time pathfinding for game NPCs in RTS games like StarCraft and Age of Empires.
Path planning for robot vacuums and drones, and road network routing in car navigation systems.
Logistics delivery route optimization and puzzle solving (15-puzzle, Rubik's Cube).
Road network routing in map services using geographic indexing (H3/S2).

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Dijkstra vs A* — Dijkstra is a special case of A* where h(n)=0. It explores all directions equally and is better when no specific destination is targeted.
BFS — The shortest path algorithm for unweighted graphs. Simpler and faster than A* when there are no edge weights.
JPS (Jump Point Search) — A grid-specific A* optimization that skips symmetric paths, achieving 10–100x speedup. D* Lite is an A* variant that incrementally repairs paths in dynamic environments.

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: A* guarantees the shortest path with an admissible heuristic
Manhattan distance works best for 4-directional, Chebyshev for 8-directional movement
Compare with BFS to see how A* explores far fewer nodes
When h=0, A* behaves identically to Dijkstra's algorithm
Watch how cells with lower f-values (lighter colors) are explored first

items.q: Is A* always faster than BFS?
items.a: In most cases A* explores fewer nodes. However, with poor heuristics or very short paths, the difference may be minimal.

items.q: Which heuristic should I choose?
items.a: Manhattan for 4-directional movement, Chebyshev for 8-directional. Euclidean works for free movement but can be slightly inefficient on grids.

items.q: What's the time complexity?
items.a: Worst case O(b^d) (b=branching factor, d=depth), but with a good heuristic it's much faster than BFS in practice.

binarySearchVisualizer.title: Binary Search Visualizer
binarySearchVisualizer.description: Watch how O(log n) search halves the range each step to find a target in a sorted array

stepsGuide.description: Watch how each comparison halves the search range until the target is found or eliminated.

whatIs.title: What is Binary Search?
whatIs.description: Binary Search finds a target value in a sorted array by halving the search range at each step. With O(log n) time complexity, it vastly outperforms linear search (O(n)). For 1,000 elements it takes at most 10 comparisons; for 1,000,000 elements, just 20.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Adjust array size with the slider (10–100)
Enter a target number or click 'Random Target'
Click 'Generate Array' to create a new sorted array
Press play to watch the search step by step
Yellow = current mid, blue = active range, gray = eliminated

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Initialize the search range: left=0, right=n-1.
Compute mid = (left + right) / 2 and compare arr[mid] with the target.
If arr[mid] === target, search succeeds. If arr[mid] < target, set left = mid+1 (right half). If arr[mid] > target, set right = mid-1 (left half).
When left > right, the search fails — the value is not in the array. Each step halves the range, achieving O(log n) complexity.

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: The core principle behind database index (B-Tree) lookups — retrieving among hundreds of millions of records in O(log n).
Dictionary/phone book search (alphabetically sorted) and git bisect to binary-search commit history for bug introduction.
Sorted coordinate lookups for game hitbox detection and parametric search in competitive programming.
Provided as standard library functions (Python bisect, Java Arrays.binarySearch, C++ std::lower_bound) — used daily in production.

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Linear search O(n) vs Binary search O(log n) — For 1,000,000 elements: linear may take 1,000,000 comparisons, binary search takes at most 20.
Interpolation Search — O(log log n) when values are uniformly distributed, but degrades to O(n) on skewed distributions.
Hash lookup O(1) — Faster for single key lookups, but cannot handle range queries or order-based retrieval.

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Try searching for a value not in the array to see the range shrink to zero
Doubling the array size only adds one more comparison — feel the log!
When L and H pointers cross, the search terminates
Binary search only works on sorted arrays

items.q: Why does the array need to be sorted?
items.a: Binary search assumes that if the mid value is less than the target, the target must be to the right. Without sorting, this assumption breaks.

items.q: Why is O(log n) so fast?
items.a: For n=1,000,000 linear search may take 1,000,000 steps, but binary search takes at most 20 (log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20).

items.q: Where is it used in practice?
items.a: Database index lookups, searching sorted lists, numerical bisection, and many standard library functions like std::binary_search or Array.prototype methods.

countingSortVisualizer.title: Counting Sort Visualizer
countingSortVisualizer.description: Watch the 3-phase non-comparison sorting: count frequencies, accumulate, and place

stepsGuide.description: Observe the 3 phases: count frequencies, compute prefix sums, and place into output.

whatIs.title: What is Counting Sort?
whatIs.description: Counting Sort is a non-comparison sorting algorithm that counts the frequency of each value to sort. With O(n+k) time complexity, it's extremely fast when the value range (k) is small, and it's a stable sort.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Adjust the array size
Use the Duplicates button for input with many repeated values
Three arrays (Input/Count/Output) are displayed simultaneously
Observe the 3 phases: counting → accumulation → placement

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Find the maximum value (k) in the input array
Create a count array of size k+1 and record how many times each value appears
Transform the count array into a prefix-sum array to determine each value's output position
Iterate through the input array in reverse, placing each element at its correct position in the output
Time O(n+k), Space O(n+k)

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Sorting exam scores (range 0–100) — limited range makes it very fast
Sorting integers with a known bounded range: ages, status codes, grade levels
Used as the inner subroutine in Radix Sort (counting sort on each digit position)
Histogram generation and frequency analysis
Bitmap index construction in databases

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Comparison sorts (Bubble/Quick/Merge) — minimum O(n log n). Counting Sort bypasses this bound with O(n+k) by not comparing elements, at the cost of O(k) memory
Radix Sort — applies Counting Sort repeatedly on each digit; handles arbitrarily large integers
Bucket Sort — distributes values into interval buckets then sorts each; can handle floating-point values

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Bypasses the O(n log n) lower bound of comparison-based sorts
Wastes memory when the value range is large
Used as a subroutine in Radix Sort due to its stability
Negative values can be handled by adding an offset

items.q: When should I use it?
items.a: When the value range (k) is similar to or smaller than n (e.g., test scores 0-100, ages 0-150). Inefficient when k >> n.

items.q: Time complexity?
items.a: O(n+k) where n is array size and k is value range. Space is also O(n+k).

bstVisualizer.title: Binary Search Tree Visualizer
bstVisualizer.description: Interactive BST visualizer: learn insert, search, and delete with step-by-step animations

stepsGuide.description: Observe how each operation maintains the BST property step by step.
stepsGuide.hint: Enter a value and press Execute to start.

whatIs.title: What is a Binary Search Tree?
whatIs.description: A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a tree data structure where each node has at most two children. Key property: all values in the left subtree < parent value < all values in the right subtree. This property enables O(log n) average-case insert, search, and delete operations.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Enter a value, select an operation (Insert/Search/Delete), and press Execute
Press Play to watch the step-by-step animation
Use Random to build a random tree, or Sorted to see the worst-case degenerate tree
Use Balanced to build a height-optimal tree for comparison
Follow the Steps panel and code tab simultaneously to understand each operation

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Insert — start at the root; if the value is smaller go left, larger go right; create a new node at the first empty slot
Search — compare from the root, moving left or right; return the node if found, fail if a leaf is reached
Delete — three cases: ① leaf node: remove directly, ② one child: replace node with child, ③ two children: replace with in-order successor (minimum of right subtree) and delete the successor
Average O(log n), worst case O(n) for a degenerate (sorted-input) tree

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Foundation of database indexes (B-Tree, B+Tree)
File system directory structure management
Compiler symbol tables (variable/function name lookup)
Autocomplete features (underlying concept behind Tries)
Game leaderboards — fast score-based rank queries and updates

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: AVL Tree — adds a height-balance constraint (height difference ≤ 1) to BST; always O(log n) but incurs rotation overhead on insert/delete
Red-Black Tree — looser balance than AVL; faster for frequent inserts/deletes; used by Java's TreeMap and C++'s std::map
B-Tree — optimized for disk-based lookups; nodes store multiple keys to minimize disk I/O; the standard index structure in databases

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Inserting values in sorted order creates a degenerate (linked-list-like) tree with O(n) height
A balanced tree keeps height near log n, ensuring O(log n) for all operations
For two-child deletion, observe how the in-order successor replaces the deleted node
Compare the node count, tree height, and comparison count across different input patterns

items.q: What is the difference between a BST and a binary heap?
items.a: A BST uses left<parent<right ordering, optimized for arbitrary value search. A binary heap uses parent≥children ordering, optimized for finding min/max. Heap search for an arbitrary value is O(n).

items.q: What is the in-order successor?
items.a: When deleting a node with two children, the in-order successor is the smallest value in the right subtree. Replacing the node with its successor and deleting the successor preserves the BST property.

items.q: How do self-balancing BSTs work?
items.a: AVL trees and Red-Black trees apply rotation operations after each insert/delete to keep tree height O(log n). Java's TreeMap and C++'s std::map use Red-Black trees internally.

floodFillVisualizer.title: Flood Fill Visualization
floodFillVisualizer.description: Click like a paint bucket to learn BFS/DFS flood fill algorithm

controls.clickHint: Click any cell on the grid to start flood fill from that position

stepsGuide.hint: Click any cell on the grid to start flood fill.
stepsGuide.bfsDescription: BFS flood fill uses a queue (FIFO) to spread outward in concentric rings from the start, filling all connected cells of the same color.
stepsGuide.dfsDescription: DFS flood fill uses a stack (LIFO) to dive deep in one direction before backtracking, filling all connected cells of the same color.

whatIs.title: What is Flood Fill?
whatIs.description: Flood Fill is the algorithm behind the paint bucket tool in image editors. Starting from a clicked cell, it fills all adjacent cells of the same color with a new color. BFS spreads like ripples in water; DFS dives deep like a maze solver.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Pick a fill color from the color palette
Click any cell on the grid to start flood fill from there
Toggle BFS or DFS mode to compare traversal styles
Use the play button to watch step-by-step filling animation
Try Random, Checkerboard, or Islands patterns for different scenarios

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Record the starting pixel's color (oldColor) and change it to the new color.
BFS approach: add the start cell to a queue. Dequeue a cell, check its 4 neighbors — if a neighbor matches oldColor, change it to the new color and enqueue it.
DFS approach: use a stack or recursion to dive deep in one direction, filling same-color cells before backtracking.
Repeat until the queue (or stack) is empty. Already-filled cells are not reprocessed.

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Core algorithm for the paint bucket and magic wand tools in image editors (Photoshop, GIMP).
Used in game terrain filling (Minecraft water flow, Minesweeper blank cell auto-reveal).
Medical image segmentation (organ/tumor region detection) and GIS contour region classification.
Circuit board connected region analysis and territory calculation in board games (Go, Reversi).

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: BFS vs DFS flood fill — BFS produces a natural wave-like animation spreading level by level. DFS (recursive) risks stack overflow on large regions; iterative stack-based DFS is safer.
Connected Component Labeling — A generalization of flood fill that assigns a unique label to every connected region in an image, widely used in computer vision.
Watershed algorithm — An advanced flood fill variant specialized for image segmentation that more precisely separates boundary regions.

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: BFS fills cells in a circular wave pattern from the origin
DFS fills cells in a snake-like deep path before backtracking
Both fill the exact same cells — only the order differs
Checkerboard grids fill only 1 cell since all neighbors differ
Real use cases: Photoshop bucket tool, Minesweeper blank reveal, game map exploration

items.q: Is BFS or DFS faster for flood fill?
items.a: Both fill the same number of cells. BFS fills in shortest-path order. DFS risks stack overflow for large areas, so iterative implementation (explicit stack) is recommended.

items.q: Where is flood fill used in practice?
items.a: Image editors (paint bucket), Minesweeper (revealing blank cells), game map traversal, connected-component labeling, and territory calculation in board games like Go or Reversi.

items.q: Can it fill diagonally?
items.a: Yes — simply define 8 neighbors instead of 4. Paint programs typically use 8-directional fill. The algorithm itself doesn't change, only which cells count as 'adjacent'.

stackQueueVisualizer.title: Stack & Queue Visualizer
stackQueueVisualizer.description: Interactively learn how Stack (LIFO) and Queue (FIFO) work
stackQueueVisualizer.demoMode: Demo mode — use playback controls to step through

steps.hint: Press an operation button or run the auto demo.
steps.lifoDesc: Last In, First Out — like a stack of plates, you always take from the top.
steps.fifoDesc: First In, First Out — like a queue of people, the first one in is the first one out.
steps.stackUses: DFS traversal, function call stack, bracket matching, Undo/Redo, expression evaluation
steps.queueUses: BFS traversal, print queue, event loop, cache eviction, process scheduling

whatIs.title: What are Stack & Queue?
whatIs.description: Stack and Queue are the most fundamental linear data structures. A Stack is LIFO (Last In First Out) — the most recently inserted element is removed first. A Queue is FIFO (First In First Out) — the earliest inserted element is removed first. Both are essential building blocks used throughout computer science: DFS/BFS traversal, function call stacks, event handling, and more.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Enter a number and click Push (Stack) or Enqueue (Queue) to add an element
Pop (Stack) removes from the TOP; Dequeue (Queue) removes from the FRONT
Run the auto demo to compare LIFO and FIFO side by side, step by step
Use the playback controls to move forward and backward through each step
Check the Code tab for a JavaScript implementation you can copy

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Stack (LIFO) — Push: add element to the top; Pop: remove and return the top element; Peek: inspect the top without removing. Implemented with an array or linked list
Queue (FIFO) — Enqueue: add element to the back; Dequeue: remove and return the front element; Peek: inspect the front. Implemented with a circular array or linked list
All operations are O(1)

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Stack — browser back/forward navigation, function call stack (recursion), Ctrl+Z undo, bracket matching, postfix expression evaluator
Queue — printer job queue, web server request handling, BFS traversal, message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ), keyboard input buffer

comparison.title: Similar Data Structures
items: Deque (Double-Ended Queue) — supports insertion and removal at both ends; a generalization of both stack and queue
Priority Queue — like a queue but elements dequeue in priority order rather than arrival order; typically implemented with a heap
Circular Queue — array-based queue that eliminates wasted space by wrapping around; ideal for fixed-size buffers

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Stack: push 10→20→30, then pop gives 30→20→10 (LIFO — last in, first out)
Queue: enqueue 10→20→30, then dequeue gives 10→20→30 (FIFO — first in, first out)
DFS uses a stack internally; BFS uses a queue internally
JavaScript's Call Stack is literally a stack data structure
A linked-list implementation makes dequeue O(1) instead of O(n)

items.q: What's the key difference between Stack and Queue?
items.a: The order of removal. A stack removes the most recently added element (TOP), while a queue removes the earliest added element (FRONT). Given the same insertion order, the removal order is the exact opposite.

items.q: Can I implement a stack/queue with a JavaScript array?
items.a: Yes. A stack uses push() and pop() for O(1) operations. A queue can use push() and shift(), but shift() is O(n). For performance-critical code, use a linked-list or circular buffer implementation.

items.q: What is a Deque?
items.a: A Double-Ended Queue (Deque) supports insertion and removal at both ends. It generalizes both stack and queue. JavaScript arrays act as a deque since they support push, pop, shift, and unshift.

radixSortVisualizer.title: Radix Sort Visualizer
radixSortVisualizer.description: Watch LSD Radix Sort distribute and collect elements through 10 buckets digit by digit

stepsGuide.description: Observe how elements are distributed into 10 buckets (0-9) and collected back in order for each digit pass.

whatIs.title: What is Radix Sort?
whatIs.description: Radix Sort is a non-comparison sorting algorithm that sorts by individual digit positions. The LSD (Least Significant Digit) approach starts from the lowest digit (ones place) and repeatedly applies counting sort up to the highest digit. Time complexity O(d×n) makes it very fast when the number of digits (d) is small, and it is a stable sort.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Adjust array size and generate input with random or same-digits buttons
Press play to start the LSD Radix Sort animation
Observe elements distributed into buckets 0-9 and collected back in order each pass
The highlighted digit box shows the current sorting digit position

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Start from the least significant digit (ones place)
Distribute each element into one of 10 buckets (0–9) based on the current digit
Collect elements from the buckets back into the array in order (0 to 9)
Advance to the next digit and repeat distribute + collect
After completing the most significant digit, the array is fully sorted — O(d × n)

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: ZIP code sorting — fixed digit count makes it near O(n)
Bulk sorting of integers/strings with fixed width: phone numbers, IP addresses
Card sorters (IBM punch-card era) — Radix Sort is historically one of the oldest sorting methods
Parallel GPU sorting — Radix Sort parallelizes extremely well
Bulk integer key index construction in databases

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Quick Sort / Merge Sort O(n log n) — comparison-based sorts are general-purpose; Radix Sort is faster when d×n < n log n (short keys)
Counting Sort — the inner subroutine used at each digit pass of Radix Sort
MSD (Most Significant Digit) Radix Sort — processes digits from the highest down; supports early termination but requires recursion

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: LSD sorts from lowest digit first — stability is required for correctness
Each pass is a Counting Sort O(n+10)=O(n), making the total O(d×n)
Compare same-digits (fixed d) vs random (variable d) to see how d affects speed
Even a large number range is fast if digits (d) are few (e.g. 64-bit integers d=19)

items.q: LSD vs MSD Radix Sort?
items.a: LSD (Least Significant Digit first) is simpler and naturally stable. MSD (Most Significant Digit first) works recursively and is better suited for string sorting. This visualizer uses LSD.

items.q: When is Radix Sort fast?
items.a: When the number of digits (d) is fixed or small (e.g. phone numbers, zip codes, dates YYYYMMDD). It beats comparison sorts when d×n < n log n.

hashTableVisualizer.title: Hash Table Visualizer
hashTableVisualizer.description: Observe how hash collisions are resolved step by step with chaining and open addressing

strategy.chainingDesc: On collision, append to a linked list in the same bucket
strategy.linearProbingDesc: On collision, scan next slots sequentially (+1, +2, ...)
strategy.quadraticProbingDesc: On collision, probe with quadratic steps (+1², +2², ...)

stepsGuide.description: Enter a key and press Insert/Search to observe the hash function → bucket mapping process.
stepsGuide.hint: Enter a key and press Insert or Search to begin.

whatIs.title: What is a Hash Table?
whatIs.description: A hash table stores key-value pairs with O(1) average-case insert, lookup, and delete. A hash function maps keys to bucket indices; collisions (two keys mapping to the same index) are resolved by chaining or open addressing. JavaScript's Object and Map, Python's dict, and Java's HashMap are all hash table implementations.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Choose a collision strategy: Chaining, Linear Probing, or Quadratic Probing
Adjust the table size — smaller tables cause more collisions
Enter a key and press Insert to watch the hash → bucket assignment
Use Batch Insert to populate the table with multiple random keys
Observe how the same bucket handles multiple keys in each strategy

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Feed the key into a hash function to produce an integer hash value
Take the hash value modulo the array size to determine the bucket index
Collision resolution — Chaining: store multiple entries in the same bucket as a linked list. Open addressing: probe for an empty slot (linear, quadratic, or double hashing)
When the load factor rises, rehash by expanding the array and redistributing all entries
Average O(1) insert, lookup, and delete

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: JavaScript's Object/Map, Python's dict, Java's HashMap — the core data structure of every modern language
Database hash indexes optimized for exact-match queries
Cache systems (Redis, Memcached) for key-value storage
Blockchain hash chains and Merkle trees
DNS cache — mapping domain names to IP addresses

comparison.title: Similar Data Structures
items: BST (Binary Search Tree) — preserves key ordering (sorted traversal possible) but averages O(log n); hash table is O(1) but unordered
Trie — specialized for string keys; prefix search in O(m) (m = key length); ideal for autocomplete
Bloom Filter — probabilistic hash structure; can definitively say 'not present' but may give false positives for 'present'; used for large-scale duplicate detection

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Performance degrades quickly above a load factor of 0.7 — resizing is needed
Chaining supports load factor > 1; open addressing requires < 1
Linear probing is simple but suffers from primary clustering
Quadratic probing reduces clustering but works best with prime table sizes
Java HashMap auto-resizes at load factor 0.75, doubling the capacity

items.q: What happens with a bad hash function?
items.a: Many collisions occur, degrading O(1) average to O(n) worst case. A good hash function distributes keys evenly. Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256) and data-structure hashes (MurmurHash) are designed for different goals.

items.q: Chaining vs open addressing — when to use which?
items.a: Chaining: better when deletions are frequent or load factor is high; each bucket is a dynamic list with memory overhead. Open addressing: cache-friendly (contiguous memory), more memory-efficient, but needs low load factor. Java uses chaining; Python uses open addressing (compact tables).

items.q: Hash table vs tree map (BST)?
items.a: Hash table: O(1) average lookup, no ordering. Tree map: O(log n) lookup, keys kept sorted. Choose hash table for fast lookup without ordering; choose tree map when range queries or sorted iteration are needed.

kruskalVisualizer.title: Kruskal's MST Visualization
kruskalVisualizer.description: Learn the greedy algorithm that builds a Minimum Spanning Tree by selecting edges in weight order

stepsGuide.description: Watch Kruskal's algorithm select edges by weight to build the MST.

whatIs.title: What is Kruskal's Algorithm?
whatIs.description: Kruskal's algorithm is a greedy algorithm that finds a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) for a weighted undirected graph. Invented by Joseph Kruskal in 1956, it connects all vertices with minimum total edge weight. It uses the Union-Find data structure to efficiently detect cycles.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Click 'New Graph' to generate a random weighted graph
Press play to sort edges by weight and start selection
Each edge is checked for cycles using Union-Find
Edges without cycles are added to MST (green), others are skipped (red)
Drag nodes to adjust the graph layout

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Kruskal's is edge-centric, while Prim's is vertex-centric
Kruskal's is more efficient for sparse graphs with fewer edges
Union-Find with path compression and union by rank achieves near-O(1) operations
An MST always has exactly V-1 edges (V = number of vertices)

items.q: Kruskal's vs Prim's — when to use which?
items.a: Kruskal's sorts edges and is O(E log E), better for sparse graphs. Prim's expands from a vertex and is O(V^2) or O(E log V) with a heap, better for dense graphs.

items.q: Is the MST unique?
items.a: If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique. If some edges have equal weights, multiple MSTs may exist.

topologicalSortVisualizer.title: Topological Sort Visualization
topologicalSortVisualizer.description: Learn Kahn's BFS-based algorithm for ordering vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)

stepsGuide.description: Watch Kahn's algorithm track in-degrees and determine topological order.

whatIs.title: What is Topological Sort?
whatIs.description: Topological Sort orders all vertices of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u→v, vertex u comes before v. It determines the execution order of tasks with dependencies. Kahn's algorithm uses in-degree tracking with BFS.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Click 'New DAG' to generate a random directed acyclic graph
The number badge next to each node shows its in-degree (incoming edges)
Nodes with in-degree 0 enter the queue first
When a node is processed, outgoing edges are removed and neighbor in-degrees decrease
The green badge below processed nodes shows their topological order number

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Topological sort is only possible for DAGs — cycles make it impossible
The result may not be unique (multiple valid orderings exist)
Build systems (Make, Gradle) use topological sort for dependency resolution
Course prerequisite planning and project scheduling also use topological sort

items.q: DFS-based vs Kahn's algorithm?
items.a: Kahn's uses in-degree BFS and naturally detects cycles. DFS-based uses reverse post-order and needs separate cycle detection (visited state tracking). Both are O(V+E).

items.q: Where is topological sort used?
items.a: Build system compilation order, package manager dependency resolution, spreadsheet cell evaluation order, course prerequisite checking, and project management (PERT/CPM).

unionFindVisualizer.title: Union-Find Visualization
unionFindVisualizer.description: Learn the Disjoint Set data structure with path compression and union by rank optimization

stepsGuide.description: Watch Union-Find perform Union/Find operations with path compression optimization.
stepsGuide.init: Initialize each node as its own set

whatIs.title: What is Union-Find?
whatIs.description: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) is a data structure for efficiently managing disjoint sets. It supports Find (check if two elements are in the same set) and Union (merge two sets) in nearly O(1) time. It is essential for Kruskal's MST, network connectivity, image processing, and more.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Use the node count slider to adjust the number of elements
Click 'New Operations' to generate random Union/Find operations
Union(a,b) merges two sets, Find(a) finds the root
Same-colored nodes belong to the same set
Watch path compression flatten the tree structure

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Without path compression, trees become deep and Find is O(n)
Union by rank attaches smaller trees under larger ones to minimize height
Path compression + union by rank = inverse Ackermann α(n) ≈ O(1)
Union-Find is essential for cycle detection in Kruskal's MST

items.q: Do I need both path compression and union by rank?
items.a: Using just one gives O(log n), but both together achieve O(α(n)) which is practically constant. In practice, both are typically used.

items.q: Real-world applications of Union-Find?
items.a: Network connectivity checking, image segmentation (connected component labeling), Kruskal's MST cycle detection, social network community detection, and equivalence relation determination.

bellmanFordVisualizer.title: Bellman-Ford Shortest Path Visualization
bellmanFordVisualizer.description: Learn the algorithm that finds shortest paths in graphs with negative weights and detects negative cycles

stepsGuide.description: Watch Bellman-Ford relax all edges V-1 times to find shortest paths.

whatIs.title: What is Bellman-Ford?
whatIs.description: The Bellman-Ford algorithm finds shortest paths from a single source to all other vertices. Unlike Dijkstra's, it handles negative weight edges and can detect negative cycles. It works by relaxing all edges V-1 times.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Click 'New Graph' to generate a directed weighted graph
Check 'Allow Negative Weights' to include negative edges
Use the source dropdown to change the starting vertex
The badge below each node shows current shortest distance from source
Red edges indicate negative weights

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Dijkstra fails with negative weights, but Bellman-Ford handles them correctly
If updates still occur after V-1 iterations, a negative cycle exists
Time complexity is O(VE), slower than Dijkstra's O(E log V)
SPFA is a queue-optimized variant of Bellman-Ford

items.q: Bellman-Ford vs Dijkstra — when to use which?
items.a: Dijkstra is faster (O(E log V)) when there are no negative edges. Bellman-Ford is needed when negative edges exist or negative cycle detection is required (O(VE)). The RIP routing protocol uses a Bellman-Ford variant.

items.q: Why V-1 iterations?
items.a: A shortest path has at most V-1 edges. Each iteration correctly determines at least one more edge's shortest distance, so V-1 iterations cover all shortest paths.

fibonacciDpVisualizer.title: Fibonacci DP Visualization
fibonacciDpVisualizer.description: Learn DP fundamentals by comparing naive recursion vs memoization vs tabulation

stepsGuide.description: Click any step to jump to that point.
stepsGuide.hint: Press Run to start.

whatIs.title: What is Fibonacci DP?
whatIs.description: Compare three ways to compute Fibonacci numbers (0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...). Naive recursion recalculates identical subproblems yielding O(2^n). Memoization (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up) eliminate redundant work for O(n).

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Select an algorithm mode (Naive/Memoization/Tabulation)
Adjust N with the slider (Naive: 0-10, DP: 0-15)
Press Run or use playback controls to animate
Step forward/backward to examine each call
Check the Code tab to see which line is executing

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Naive recursion: directly calls fib(n-1) + fib(n-2), creating an exponentially growing call tree (fib(10) = 177 calls)
Memoization: caches computed values in a memo object. Repeated fib(k) calls return in O(1), pruning entire subtrees
Tabulation: fills dp[0]=0, dp[1]=1, then dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] sequentially
Both DP approaches run in O(n) time, O(n) space. Tabulation avoids recursion stack overflow

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: The quintessential DP intro example, frequently appears in coding interviews
Fibonacci heaps and golden-ratio algorithms use Fibonacci numbers
Memoization pattern is used in React.memo, useMemo, Python's @lru_cache
Tabulation pattern is the foundation of Knapsack, LCS, edit distance DP problems

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Run Naive mode with N=8 to feel how massive the call tree gets
In Memoization mode, notice yellow 'memo' nodes — branches are pruned
Compare call counts across all three modes to quantify DP's power

items.q: What's the difference between memoization and tabulation?
items.a: Memoization is top-down (recursion + caching), tabulation is bottom-up (iteration + table). Same result, but tabulation avoids recursion stack overflow for large N.

items.q: Why is Naive limited to N=10?
items.a: At N=10 there are 177 calls. N=20 produces 21,891, N=30 about 2.7 million — enough to freeze the browser.

items.q: Can we reduce O(n) space?
items.a: Yes, by keeping only the last two values you get O(1) space. But problems requiring traceback (like Knapsack) need the full table.

knapsackVisualizer.title: Knapsack Problem Visualization
knapsackVisualizer.description: Find the maximum value combination within a weight limit — a classic DP problem

stepsGuide.description: Click any step to jump to that point.
stepsGuide.hint: Press Run to start.

whatIs.title: What is the Knapsack Problem?
whatIs.description: An optimization problem where you pack items into a weight-limited knapsack to maximize value. In the 0/1 variant, each item is either included (1) or excluded (0). dp[i][w] stores the maximum value using the first i items with capacity w.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Select a preset (Camping/Treasure/Study) or adjust capacity
Press Run to start filling the DP table
Hover over cells to see dp[i][w] values
During traceback, selected items are highlighted
The Steps tab shows include/exclude decisions

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-w_i] + v_i): compare including vs excluding item i
If item weight exceeds capacity, dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w] (can't include)
After filling the table, trace back from dp[n][W] to find selected items
Time complexity O(n*W), space O(n*W). Pseudo-polynomial algorithm

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Investment portfolio optimization — maximize returns within budget
Cargo loading — maximize value within truck/container weight limits
Cloud resource allocation — schedule jobs within CPU/memory constraints
Ad budget allocation — maximize impressions within budget

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Start with the Camping preset for a small example
The key insight is comparing include vs exclude values at each cell
During traceback, dp[i][w] != dp[i-1][w] means item i was selected

items.q: 0/1 Knapsack vs Fractional Knapsack?
items.a: 0/1 requires DP (items can't be split). Fractional allows splitting items and can be solved greedily by value-to-weight ratio.

items.q: Why is it pseudo-polynomial?
items.a: O(n*W) depends on the value of W, not its bit-length. If W has b bits, the actual complexity is O(n*2^b), which is exponential in input size.

lcsVisualizer.title: LCS (Longest Common Subsequence) Visualization
lcsVisualizer.description: Find the longest common subsequence of two strings using a DP table

stepsGuide.description: Click any step to jump to that point.
stepsGuide.hint: Press Run to start.

whatIs.title: What is LCS?
whatIs.description: LCS (Longest Common Subsequence) finds the longest subsequence common to two strings while maintaining order. A subsequence doesn't need to be contiguous. Example: LCS of 'ABCDE' and 'ACE' is 'ACE' (length 3).

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Select a preset or enter two strings (max 10 chars each)
Press Run to start filling the DP table
Green cells indicate character matches, red cells indicate mismatches
Arrow directions show the traceback path
After traceback, the LCS string appears at the bottom

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: If str1[i] == str2[j]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 (diagonal arrow)
If str1[i] != str2[j]: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) (up or left arrow)
dp[m][n] is the LCS length. Follow arrows backward to construct the LCS string
Time complexity O(m*n), space O(m*n)

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: git diff — file change comparison uses LCS variants
DNA/RNA sequence alignment in bioinformatics
Plagiarism detection — finding common passages between documents
Auto-merge — 3-way merge in source code uses LCS-based algorithms

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Start with the 'ABCDE' / 'ACE' preset for a simple example
Diagonal arrows correspond to LCS characters
Follow the yellow traceback path to see how the LCS is constructed

items.q: Subsequence vs substring?
items.a: A subsequence maintains order but needn't be contiguous. A substring must be contiguous. 'ACE' is a subsequence of 'ABCDE' but not a substring.

items.q: Can there be multiple LCS?
items.a: Yes, multiple LCS of the same length can exist. This visualization shows one based on arrow directions. Finding all requires exploring branches during traceback.

kmpVisualizer.title: KMP Pattern Matching Visualization
kmpVisualizer.description: O(n+m) string pattern matching using the failure function

stepsGuide.description: Click any step to jump to that point.
stepsGuide.hint: Press Run to start.

whatIs.title: What is KMP?
whatIs.description: KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) finds pattern occurrences in text in O(n+m) time. Unlike the naive O(n*m) approach, it uses a 'failure function' to skip unnecessary comparisons on mismatch.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Select a preset or enter custom text and pattern
Press Run to start Phase 1 (failure function) then Phase 2 (search)
Watch the failure table (bottom) being filled
During search, observe the pattern sliding along the text
Match positions are highlighted in green

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Phase 1 (Failure function): Pre-computes prefix-suffix match lengths for the pattern. failure[i] is the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix
Phase 2 (Search): Compares text and pattern character by character. On match, both advance
On mismatch: set pi = failure[pi-1] to efficiently shift the pattern, reusing already-matched prefix
When the full pattern matches (pi == m), record the match and use failure to continue searching

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Text editor Find/Replace functionality
Network Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) pattern matching
DNA sequence pattern searching in bioinformatics
Compiler lexical analysis

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: The failure function is the key — understand why it enables skipping
Hand-compute the failure function for 'ABABC' = [0,0,1,2,0]
Think about why pi = failure[pi-1] is correct on mismatch

items.q: KMP vs Rabin-Karp vs Boyer-Moore?
items.a: KMP: guaranteed O(n+m), uses failure function. Rabin-Karp: hash-based, average O(n+m), worst O(nm). Boyer-Moore: compares from right, often fastest in practice. Choose KMP when worst-case guarantee is needed.

items.q: Why is it called 'failure' function?
items.a: It tells you where to go back on a mismatch (failure). Also known as 'partial match table' or 'prefix function'.

trieVisualizer.title: Trie Visualization
trieVisualizer.description: A tree-based data structure for fast string lookup and autocomplete

stepsGuide.description: Click any step to jump to that point.
stepsGuide.hint: Select an operation and press Execute.

whatIs.title: What is a Trie?
whatIs.description: A Trie (prefix tree) stores a set of strings character-by-character in a tree. Shared prefixes save memory, and insert/search/autocomplete all run in O(m) where m is the string length. Word-end nodes are shown with double circles.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: The initial trie contains CAR, CARD, CARE, CAT, DO, DOG, DONE
Select an operation (Insert/Search/Autocomplete) and enter a word
Insert: creates new nodes and marks word end
Search: follows path and checks existence
Autocomplete: navigates to prefix end, then collects all words below

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Insert: traverse from root, creating child nodes for each character, mark the final node as word-end
Search: follow characters from root. If a child is missing, return 'not found'. If reached end, check isEnd flag
Autocomplete: navigate to prefix-end node, then DFS to collect all words in the subtree
Time complexity: all operations O(m). Autocomplete is O(m + total output length)

realWorld.title: Real-World Applications
items: Search engine autocomplete (Google, Bing)
Smartphone keyboard word prediction
IP routing tables (longest prefix matching)
Spell checkers and dictionaries

tips.title: Learning Tips
items: Try autocomplete with 'CA' — you'll get CAR, CARD, CARE, CAT showing prefix sharing
Insert 'DARE' to see a new D-A-R-E path separate from DO
Double circles mark word-end nodes — if R in C-A-R has a double circle, 'CAR' exists

items.q: Trie vs Hash Table?
items.a: Hash tables offer O(1) exact lookup but can't do prefix search/autocomplete. Tries excel at prefix operations but use more memory. Choose Trie for autocomplete, Hash Table for exact lookup.

items.q: How to reduce memory?
items.a: Compressed tries (Patricia/radix trees) merge single-child nodes to save space. Using arrays instead of hash maps for children reduces pointer overhead.

convexHullVisualizer.title: Convex Hull Visualizer
convexHullVisualizer.description: Visualize the Graham Scan algorithm building a convex hull step by step

controls.clickToAdd: Click the canvas to add points. Drag points to reposition.

stepsGuide.description: Watch how Graham Scan uses a stack to build the convex hull.

whatIs.title: What is Convex Hull?
whatIs.description: The convex hull of a set of points is the smallest convex polygon containing all points. Graham Scan computes it in O(n log n).

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Adjust point count or click canvas to add points
Use Random or Circle buttons to generate points
Press play to watch Graham Scan step by step
Orange is pivot, purple is stack, yellow is current point
Drag points to see how the hull changes

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Find the lowest point as pivot
Sort points by polar angle from pivot
Push points onto stack; pop on clockwise turns
Cross product determines turn direction
Time: O(n log n). Space: O(n)

realWorld.title: Applications
items: Collision detection in games/CAD
GIS service area computation
Image processing contour analysis
Robotics obstacle avoidance

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Graham Scan vs Jarvis March — O(n log n) vs O(nh)
Quickhull — divide-and-conquer, fast in practice
Andrew Monotone Chain — simpler implementation

tips.title: Tips
items: Circle placement keeps all points on hull
More interior points mean more pops
Collinear points are removed (cross product = 0)
Drag points to build intuition

items.q: Convex vs concave hull?
items.a: Convex hull has all angles ≤ 180°. Concave hull (alpha shape) wraps tighter.

items.q: Time complexity?
items.a: O(n log n), dominated by sorting.

items.q: 3D convex hull?
items.a: Yes, Quickhull 3D runs in O(n log n).

voronoiVisualizer.title: Voronoi Diagram Visualizer
voronoiVisualizer.description: Watch how each pixel is assigned to its nearest site, forming a Voronoi partition

controls.clickToAdd: Click the canvas to add a site.

stepsGuide.description: The sweep line moves top to bottom, assigning each pixel to its nearest site.

whatIs.title: What is a Voronoi Diagram?
whatIs.description: A Voronoi diagram partitions a plane into regions around seed points where every point is closest to its site.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: Adjust site count or click canvas to add sites
Use Random or Grid buttons
Press play to watch sweep animation
Regions are colored by site; dark lines are boundaries

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: Compute distance from each pixel to all sites
Assign pixel to nearest site
Mark boundary where nearest site changes
Brute force O(n*w*h), Fortune O(n log n)
This visualization uses brute-force for clarity

realWorld.title: Applications
items: Urban planning — nearest facility assignment
Game development — map generation
Network design — cell tower coverage
Meteorology — spatial interpolation

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Voronoi vs Delaunay Triangulation — dual structures
Fortune Sweep Line — optimal O(n log n)
k-d Tree — nearest neighbor search

tips.title: Tips
items: Even spacing produces similar-sized regions
Clustering creates size contrasts
Voronoi edges are perpendicular bisectors

items.q: Voronoi-Delaunay relationship?
items.a: Dual structures. Delaunay circumcenters become Voronoi vertices.

items.q: Fortune algorithm?
items.a: O(n log n) sweep line with beach line and event queue.

items.q: 3D extension?
items.a: Yes, produces polyhedral cells.

stepsGuide.step2: DDA steps along grid until ray hits a wall
stepsGuide.step3: Calculate perpendicular distance with fisheye correction
stepsGuide.step4: Draw column height inversely proportional to distance

whatIs.title: What is Raycasting?
whatIs.description: Raycasting creates a 3D-like first-person view from 2D map data. Popularized by Wolfenstein 3D (1992).

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: WASD or arrow keys to move/rotate
Use touch buttons on mobile
Edit Map to add/remove walls
Watch minimap for ray distribution
Reset Map to restore defaults

howItWorks.title: How It Works
items: FOV divided into columns, one ray per column
DDA checks wall at each grid crossing
Perpendicular distance with fisheye correction
Shorter distance = taller wall column
Different shading for vertical/horizontal walls

realWorld.title: Applications
items: Early FPS games — Wolfenstein 3D, DOOM
Robot LiDAR scanning
Autonomous vehicle sensor simulation
Architecture lighting analysis

comparison.title: Similar Algorithms
items: Raycasting vs Ray Tracing — column-based vs pixel-based with reflections
BSP — DOOM rendering order
Rasterization — modern GPU triangle-based rendering

tips.title: Tips
items: Walk close to walls to see perspective projection
Observe fan-shaped rays on minimap — that is FOV
Wall shading differences create depth perception
Edit map to create mazes

items.q: What is DDA?
items.a: Digital Differential Analyzer — steps along grid checking for wall intersections.

items.q: Why fisheye correction?
items.a: Edge rays travel farther; cos(angle_diff) corrects the distortion.

items.q: Still used today?
items.a: In 2D grid games, yes. Ray tracing (RTX) is the modern extension.
